# Finding Terms of a Sequence
Each of Exercies 1-6 gives a formula for the $n$th term $a_n$ of a sequence
$\{a_n\}$. Find the values of $a_1, a_2, a_3$, and $a_4$.

1. $a_n = \frac{1 - n}{n^2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = \frac{1 - 1}{1^2} &= 0 \\\\
a_2 = \frac{1 - 2}{2^2} &= -\frac{1}{4} \\\\
a_3 = \frac{1 - 3}{3^2} &= -\frac{2}{9} \\\\
a_4 = \frac{1 - 4}{4^2} &= -\frac{3}{16}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r exercise_1, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p01.png")
```

2. $a_n = \frac{1}{n!}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = \frac{1}{1!} &= 1 \\\\
a_2 = \frac{1}{2!} &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_3 = \frac{1}{3!} &= \frac{1}{6} \\\\
a_4 = \frac{1}{4!} &= \frac{1}{24}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r exercise_2, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p02.png")
```

3. $a_n = \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n - 1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = \frac{(-1)^{1 + 1}}{2(1) - 1} &= 1 \\\\
a_2 = \frac{(-1)^{2 + 1}}{2(2) - 1} &= -\frac{1}{3} \\\\
a_3 = \frac{(-1)^{3 + 1}}{2(3) - 1} &= \frac{1}{5} \\\\
a_4 = \frac{(-1)^{4 + 1}}{2(4) - 1} &= -\frac{1}{7}
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r exercise_3, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p03.png")
```

4. $a_n = 2 + (-1)^n$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = 2 + (-1)^1 &= 1 \\\\
a_2 = 2 + (-1)^2 &= 3 \\\\
a_3 = 2 + (-1)^3 &= 1 \\\\
a_4 = 2 + (-1)^4 &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r exercise_4, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p04.png")
```

5. $a_n = \frac{2^n}{2^{n+1}}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = \frac{2^1}{2^{1 + 1}} = \frac{2}{4}   &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_2 = \frac{2^2}{2^{2 + 1}} = \frac{4}{8}   &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_3 = \frac{2^3}{2^{3 + 1}} = \frac{8}{16}  &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_4 = \frac{2^4}{2^{4 + 1}} = \frac{16}{32} &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r exercise_4, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p05.png")
```

6. $a_n = \frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 = \frac{2^1 - 1}{2^1} &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_2 = \frac{2^2 - 1}{2^2} &= \frac{3}{4} \\\\
a_3 = \frac{2^3 - 1}{2^3} &= \frac{7}{8} \\\\
a_4 = \frac{2^4 - 1}{2^4} &= \frac{15}{16} \\\\
\end{aligned}
$$

Each of Exercises 7-12 gives the first term or two of a sequence along with a
recursion formula for the remaining terms. Write out the first ten terms of the
sequence.

7. $a_1 = 1, a_{n+1} = a_n + (1/2^n)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= 1 \\\\
a_2 &= a_1 + (1/2^1) &= 1 + 1/2 &= 3/2 \\\\
a_3 &= a_2 + (1/2^2) &= 3/2 + 1/4 &= 7/4 \\\\
a_4 &= a_3 + (1/2^3) &= 7/4 + 1/8 &= 15/8 \\\\
a_5 &= a_4 + (1/2^4) &= 15/8 + 1/16 &= 31/16 \\\\
a_6 &= a_5 + (1/2^5) &= 31/16 + 1/32 &= 63/32 \\\\
a_7 &= a_6 + (1/2^6) &= 63/32 + 1/64 &= 127/64 \\\\
a_8 &= a_7 + (1/2^7) &= 127/64 + 1/128 &= 255/128 \\\\
a_9 &= a_8 + (1/2^8) &= 255/128 + 1/256 &= 511/256 \\\\
a_{10} &= a_9 + (1/2^9) &= 511/256 + 1/512 &= 1023/512
\end{aligned}
$$

8. $a_1 = 1, a_{n+1} = a_n / (n + 1)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= 1 \\\\
a_2 &= a_1 / (1 + 1) &= 1/2 \\\\
a_3 &= a_2 / (2 + 1) &= 1/6 \\\\
a_4 &= a_3 / (3 + 1) &= 1/24 \\\\
a_5 &= a_4 / (4 + 1) &= 1/120 \\\\
a_6 &= a_5 / (5 + 1) &= 1/720 \\\\
a_7 &= a_6 / (6 + 1) &= 1/5040 \\\\
a_8 &= a_7 / (7 + 1) &= 1/40320 \\\\
a_9 &= a_8 / (8 + 1) &= 1/362880 \\\\
a_{10} &= a_9 / (9 + 1) &= 1/3628800
\end{aligned}
$$

9. $a_1 = 2, a_{n + 1} = (-1)^{n+1}a_n/2$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 & \quad &= 2 \\\\
a_2 &= (-1)^{1 + 1}2/2 &= 1 \\\\
a_3 &= (-1)^{2 + 1}1/2 &= -\frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_4 &= (-1)^{3 + 1}(-1/2)/2 &= -\frac{1}{4} \\\\
a_5 &= (-1)^{4 + 1}(-1/4)/2 &= \frac{1}{8} \\\\
a_6 &= (-1)^{5 + 1}(1/8)/2 &= \frac{1}{16} \\\\
a_7 &= (-1)^{6 + 1}(1/16)/2 &= -\frac{1}{32} \\\\
a_8 &= (-1)^{7 + 1}(-1/32)/2 &= -\frac{1}{64} \\\\
a_9 &= (-1)^{8 + 1}(-1/64)/2 &= \frac{1}{128} \\\\
a_{10} &= (-1)^{9 + 1}(1/128)/2 &= \frac{1}{256} \\\\
\end{aligned}
$$

10. $a_1 = -2, a_{n+1} = na_n/(n+1)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= \quad &= -2 \\\\
a_2 &= (1)(-2)/(1 + 1) &= -1 \\\\
a_3 &= (2)(-1)/(2 + 1) &= -\frac{2}{3} \\\\
a_4 &= (3)(-2/3)/(3 + 1) &= -\frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_5 &= (4)(-1/2)/(4 + 1) &= -\frac{2}{5} \\\\
a_6 &= (5)(-2/5)/(5 + 1) &= -\frac{1}{3} \\\\
a_7 &= (6)(-1/3)/(6 + 1) &= -\frac{2}{7} \\\\
a_8 &= (7)(-2/7)/(7 + 1) &= -\frac{1}{4} \\\\
a_9 &= (8)(-1/4)/(8 + 1) &= -\frac{2}{9} \\\\
a_{10} &= (9)(-2/9)/(9 + 1) &= -\frac{1}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

11. $a_1 = a_2 = 1, a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 & \quad &= 1 \\\\
a_2 & \quad &= 1 \\\\
a_3 &= 1 + 1 &= 2 \\\\
a_4 &= 2 + 1 &= 3 \\\\
a_5 &= 3 + 2 &= 5 \\\\
a_6 &= 5 + 3 &= 8 \\\\
a_7 &= 8 + 5 &= 13 \\\\
a_8 &= 13 + 8 &= 21 \\\\
a_9 &= 21 + 13 &= 34 \\\\
a_{10} &= 34 + 21 &= 55
\end{aligned}
$$

12. $a_1 = 2, a_2 = -1, a_{n+2} = a_{n+1}/a_n$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 & \quad &= 2 \\\\
a_2 & \quad &= -1 \\\\
a_3 & \quad &= -\frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_4 &= (-1/2)/(-1) &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_5 &= (1/2)/(-1/2) &= -1 \\\\
a_6 &= (-1)/(1/2) &= -2 \\\\
a_7 &= (-2)/(-1) &= 2 \\\\
a_8 &= (2)/(-2) &= -1 \\\\
a_9 &= (-1)/(2) &= -\frac{1}{2} \\\\
a_{10} &= (-1/2)/(-1) &= \frac{1}{2} \\\\
\end{aligned}
$$

# Finding a Sequence's Formula
In Exercises 13-22, find a formula for the $n$th term of the sequence.

13. The sequence $1, -1, 1, -1, 1, \ldots$

$$
a_n = (-1)^{n + 1}, n \ge 1
$$

14. The sequence $-1, 1, -1, 1, -1, \ldots$

$$
a_n = (-1)^n, n \ge 1
$$

15. The sequence $1, -4, 9, -16, 25, \ldots$

$$
a_n = (-1)^{n + 1}(n^2), n \ge 1
$$

16. The sequence $1, -\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{9}, -\frac{1}{16}, \frac{1}{25}, \cdots$

$$
a_n = (-1)^{n + 1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2, n \ge 1
$$

17. The sequence $0, 3, 8 ,15, 24, \ldots$

$$
a_n = n^2-1, n \ge 1
$$

18. The sequence $-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, \ldots$

$$
a_n = n, n \ge -3
$$

19. The sequence $1, 5, 9, 13, 17, \ldots$

$$
a_n = 4n-3
$$

20. The sequence $2, 6, 10, 14, 18, \ldots$

$$
a_n = 4n-2
$$

21. The sequence $1, 0, 1, 0, 1, \ldots$

$$
a_n = \frac{1 - (-1)^n}{2}
$$

22. The sequence $0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, \ldots$

$$
a_n = \frac{2n - 1 + (-1)^n}{4}
$$

# Calculator Explorations of Limits
In Exercises 23-26, experiment with a calculator to find a value of $N$ that
will make the inequality hold for all $n > N$. Assuming that the inequality is
the one from the formal definition of the limit of a sequence, what sequence is
being considered in each case and what is its limit?

23. $\mid\sqrt[n]{0.5} - 1\mid < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_23, echo=TRUE}
n <- 1:1000
e23 <- function(n) abs(.5^(1/n) - 1) < 10^(-3)
cat("N =", (N <- which(e23(n))[1]))
```

$$
a_n = \sqrt[n]{0.5}
$$

The limit is $L = 1$

24. $\mid\sqrt[n]{n} - 1\mid < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_24, echo=TRUE}
n <- 1:20000
e24 <- function(n) abs(n^(1/n) - 1)
cat("N =", (N <- max(which(!(e24(n) < 10^(-3))))))
```

$$
a_n = \sqrt[n]{n} - 1
$$

The limit is $L = 1$

25. $(0.9)^n < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_25, echo=TRUE}
n <- 1:1000
e25 <- function(n) 0.9^n < 10^(-3)
cat("n >=", (N <- which(e25(n))[1]))
```

26. $\frac{2^n}{n!} < 10^{-7}$

```{r exercise_26, echo=TRUE}
n <- 1:1000
e26 <- function(n) (2^n)/factorial(n) < 10^(-7)
cat("N =", (N <- which(e26(n))[1]))
```

27. __Sequences generated by Newton's method.__ Newton's method, applied to a
    differentiable function $f(x)$, begins with a starting value of $x_0$ and
    constructs from it a sequence of numbers $\{x_n\}$ that under favorable
    circumstances converges to a zero of $f$. The recursion formula for the
    sequence is
$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

a. Show that the recursion formula for $f(x) = x^2 - a, a > 0$, can be written
   as $x_{n+1} = (x_n + a / x_n) / 2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{x_n^2 - a}{2x_n} \\\\
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n - \frac{a}{x_n}\right) \\\\
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{1}{2}x_n + \frac{a/x_n}{2} \\\\
x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}x_n + \frac{a/x_n}{2} \\\\
x_{n+1} = \frac{x_n + a/x_n}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b. Starting with $x_0 = 1$ and $a = 3$, calculate successive terms of the
   sequence until the display begins to repeat. What number is being
   approximated? Explain.

```{r exercise_27, echo=TRUE}
newton_seq <- function(f, fp, x0, n) {
    if (n == 0) return(x0)
    prev <- newton_seq(f, fp, x0, n - 1)
    x <- prev[length(prev)]
    c(prev, x - f(x) / fp(x))
}

f <- function(x) x^2 - 3
fp <- deriv(~ x^2 - 3, "x", function.arg = TRUE)
fp_val <- function(x) attr(fp(x), "gradient")[1]
newton_seq(f, fp_val, x0 = 1, n = 5)
```

> The number being approximated is $\sqrt{3} = `r round(sqrt(3), 6)`$.

28. Repeat part (b) of Exercise 27 with $a = 2$ in place of $a = 3$

```{r exercise_28, echo=TRUE}
f <- function(x) x^2 - 2
fp <- function(x) 2 * x
newton_seq(f, fp, x0 = 1, n = 4)
```

> The number being approximated is $\sqrt{2} = `r round(sqrt(2), 6)`$.

29. __A recursive definition of $\pi / 2$.__ If you start with $x_1 = 1$ and
    define the subsequent terms of $\{x_n\}$ by the rule $x_n = x_{n-1} +
    \cos{x_{n-1}}$, you generate a sequence that converges rapidly to $\pi/2$.
    (a) Try it. (b) Use the accompanying figure to explain why the convergence
    is so rapid.

a. Using a recursive function to approximate $\pi/2$.

```{r exercise_29}
x <- 1
approx_pi_seq <- function(x, n) {
    if (n == 0) return(x)
    n <- approx_pi_seq(x, n-1)
    x <- n[length(n)]
    c(n, x + cos(x))
}
approx_pi_seq(1, 3)
```

b. On the unit circle, the arc from $P = (\cos x_{n-1}, \sin x_{n-1})$ to $(0, 1)$
has length $\frac{\pi}{2} - x_{n-1}$, and the horizontal segment from $P$ to
the y-axis has length $\cos x_{n-1}$. Near the top of the circle the arc is
nearly horizontal, so these two lengths are nearly equal. Adding $\cos x_{n-1}$
therefore takes $x_{n-1}$ almost exactly to $\frac{\pi}{2}$. More precisely, if
$\varepsilon = \frac{\pi}{2} - x_{n-1}$, the new error is $\varepsilon -
\sin\varepsilon \approx \varepsilon^3/6$. The error is cubed at each step,
which is why the sequence matches $\pi/2$ to 15 digits after only three
iterations.

30. According to a front-page article in the December 15, 1992, issue of _The
    Wall Street Journal_, Ford Motor Company now uses about $7\frac{1}{4}$
    hours of labor to produce stampings for the average vehicle, down from an
    esitmated 15 hours in 1980. The Japanese need only about $3\frac{1}{2}$
    hours.  
>   For's improvement since 1980 represents an average decrease of 6% per year.
>   If that rate continues, then $n$ years from now Ford will use about
$$
S_n = 7.25(0.94)^n
$$

>   hours of labor to produce stampings for the average vehicle. Assuming that
>   the Japanese continue to spend $3\frac{1}{2}$ hours per vehicle, how many
>   more years will it take Ford to catch up? Find out two ways:  

>  a. Find the first term of the sequence $\{S_n\}$ that is less than or equal
      to 3.5.  

```{r exercise_29_a}
n <- 1:25
f <- function(x) 7.25 * 0.94^x
Sn <- f(n)
(n_cross <- which(Sn <= 3.5)[1])
Sn[n_cross]
```

>  b. GRAPHER Graph $f(x) = 7.25(0.94)^x$ and use TRACE to find where the graph
      crosses the line $y=3.5$.

```{r exercise_29_b}
(x_cross <- log(3.5 / 7.25) / log(0.94))
ggplot() +
    stat_function(fun = f, xlim = c(0, 25), n = 500) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 3.5, color="blue") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = x_cross, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("point", x = x_cross, y = 3.5, color = "red", size = 2) +
    labs(x = "years from now", y = "hours per vehicle")
```

> The graph crosses at $x \approx 11.77$, so Ford catches up during year 12,
> which agrees with part (a).

# Theory and Examples
In Exercises 31-34, determine if the sequence is nondecreasing and if it is
bounded from above.

31. $a_n = \frac{3n + 1}{n + 1}$

```{r exercise_31, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p31.png")
```

> The figure above demonstrates that $a_n$ is nondecreasing and is bounded from above by a_n < 3.

32. $a_n = \frac{(2n + 3)!}{(n + 1)!}$

```{r exercise_32, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p32.png")
```

> The figure above shows $a_n$ as nondecreasing but not bounded. The last point
> shows how extreme the last value is relative the the previous values of the
> sequence.

33. $a_n = \frac{2^n 3^n}{n!}$

```{r exercise_33, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/8-1-p33.png")
```
> The figure shows that $a_n$ is not nondecreasing and it is bounded from above.

34. $a_n = 2 - \frac{2}{n} - \frac{1}{2^n}$

```{r exercise_34, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}

```
> The figure shows that $a_n$ is nondecreasing and is bounded from above.

40. The first term of a sequence is $x_1 = \cos{(1)}$. The next terms are $x_2
    = x_1$ or $\cos{(2)}$, whichever is larger; and $x_3 = x_2$ or $\cos{(3)}$,
    whichever is larger (farther to the right). In general,

$$
x_{n+1} = \max \{x_n, \cos{(n + 1)}\}
$$
